context_blurb:
How can you tell whether one thing really causes another? Scientists run a controlled experiment: change one thing on purpose, keep everything else the same, and compare the results. Tests can break in a few classic ways, and spotting them lets you check claims yourself.

A variable is anything in a test that can change. The independent variable is the one the experimenter changes on purpose, and the dependent variable is the result she measures to see its effect. When fertiliser is tested on daisies, the amount given is the independent variable, their growth the dependent one, and water, sunlight and pot size, kept alike, are controlled variables. Setting something yourself does not make it controlled; controlled means held the same. The dependent variable must also measure what the question asks: if it asks about flowers or fruit, count them, for a plant's height shows something else.

Charles Darwin grew maize seedlings in pairs. One came from a seed made with another plant's pollen, the other with pollen from a second flower on the same plant, since each maize flower is male or female. Each pair shared one pot of evenly mixed soil, a plant on each side; a partition between them always faced the light so both were lit alike, and both were watered together. With soil, light and water held the same, these were controlled variables, so only the way each seed was made, the independent variable, could explain a difference in height, the dependent one. In thirteen of fifteen pairs, the plant from another plant's pollen grew taller.

A control group is something else: a whole group left without the thing being tested, but treated like the others in every other way. In the daisy test, the unfed daisies are the control group. From 1843, at Rothamsted in England, Lawes and Gilbert fed each strip of a wheat field its own fertiliser or manure, but one strip has had nothing at all ever since. Wheat is still sown on it every year, so it shows what the wheat gives with nothing added: about a tonne of grain a hectare, against ten or more on the best-fed strips.

Without a control group, a change cannot be pinned on the treatment. Marks often rise from practice alone, as people grow used to a kind of test. So if every pupil got a lucky pencil for each spelling test and the marks climbed all term, the pencil might have done nothing. Only a matching class taking the same tests with ordinary pencils could show whether it helped. Another round with every pupil holding one would not help, since nothing untreated is left to compare.

A test also breaks when two things change at once, because neither can take the credit. A cyclist who tries new tyres downhill and old ones on the flat learns nothing about tyres: the hill could explain it. Seedlings fed in brighter light than the unfed ones may have grown taller from the extra light alone, for light helps plants grow.

Around 1890 in Java, the Dutch doctor Christiaan Eijkman saw the chickens in his laboratory sicken with a nerve disease like beriberi while they ate polished white rice; unpolished rice cured them. To test the rice alone, feed one flock polished rice and a matching flock unpolished rice, with all else alike. Eijkman's trials in the early 1890s did just that: nearly all the birds on polished rice fell ill, and those on unpolished rice did not. Polished rice, it was later found, lacks thiamine, vitamin B1, and Eijkman shared a Nobel Prize in 1929.

Living things vary: even a good packet holds dead seeds and dormant ones, alive but resting, that will not sprout. So with just one seed in each group, a seed that fails may simply have been dead, and the result is left to chance. With many seeds in each group, chance failures fall on both sides and a real difference shows through. Darwin judged tests of only two to six pairs of plants nearly worthless.

Last, a result speaks only for what was tested. Francis Galton, checking Darwin's maize figures, warned that they held only within the conditions tested. If three brands of glue are tested on paper, the winner is the best of those three on paper; other brands, and wood or glass, stay untested and unknown. A fair test that finds no difference has not failed either, for no difference is a result too.
